papers.title: The Quality of Resources Used in Google AI Overviews for Health Topics
papers.venue: SocArXiv (OSF Preprints)
papers.abstract: Background: The growing number of consumers seeking health information online are increasingly offered Google AI Overviews atop their searches. Recent research has identified pitfalls of using large language models for health information generation. Objectives: To examine sources employed in generating AI overviews for minority-language queries and evaluate their quality. Methods: Query topics were derived from the Czech National Medical Library's patient information portal, entered in Google, and information about sources linked to AI overviews was collected and statistically analysed. Results: Of 145 distinct queries, 40 (27.6%) did not yield AI overviews. The remaining 105 queries produced 1,231 unique URLs (mean=11.7). General web pages were most frequent (68.9%, n=848), followed by Wikipedia (5.4%, n=66) and peer-reviewed articles (2.9%, n=35). Private-sector entities owned 55.7% of sources, public sector 29.5%, and non-profits 14.8%. Quality scores ranged from −1.5 to 7.0 (mean=1.85). Poor-quality sources comprised 28.4%, while 10.6% were excellent. Discussion: Quality variability strongly correlates with sector ownership. Public sources and structured initiatives demonstrate best practices, while private entities often introduce commercial bias and non-evidence-based content. Conclusion: Source quality for Czech health AI overviews is highly variable and sector-dependent. Rigorous quality control measures are essential for consumer safety.

papers.title: The New Frontier of Wine Search Optimization: AI Search Operations at Honig Vineyard & Winery
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Wine buyers and visitors increasingly get a single synthesized answer from Google AI, ChatGPT, Perplexity or Gemini instead of a page of links. Those answers are assembled from whatever sources the engine can retrieve and trust, and for most wineries that includes directories, tourism boards, reservation platforms and old press that the winery does not control.This paper describes how answer engines build a description of a winery, why conflicting facts across sources weaken that description, and which technical layers a winery can manage to correct it. papers.title: Where the 70% Cart Abandonment Rate Comes From: The 50 Studies Behind the Most Cited E-commerce Statistic and How AI Search Answers Repeat It
papers.venue: Knowledge Commons (Lakehead University)
papers.abstract: "About 70% of online shopping carts are abandoned" is one of the most repeated numbers in e-commerce writing. Its usual source is the Baymard Institute's list of cart abandonment studies, which reports an unweighted average of 70.22% across 50 studies published from 2006 to 2025. We rebuilt that average from the list and examined what stands behind it. The 50 studies reproduce the figure exactly. Their median study year is 2013, 33 of the 50 are from 2015 or earlier, and 6 are from 2021 or later. Thirty studies (60%) come from companies that sell cart recovery or remarketing services; their mean is 72.78%, against 66.38% for the other 20. Three companies supply 44% of the studies. Reports of the same year disagree by up to 26.7 percentage points, which points to different definitions and client bases rather than to a common measurement. A least-squares trend rises by 0.65 points a year, from 64.9% in 2006 to 77.2% in 2025. Seven reasonable ways to aggregate the same list give values from 66.4% to 77.2%. On November 6, 2026, Google's AI Overviews for four cart abandonment queries all opened with 70.22% and then stated 29 further figures from 11 other sources, including mobile rates from 76.98% to 86% and food and beverage rates from 38.16% to 82% on the same day. We conclude that 70% is a stable convention built from vendor reports, not a measured rate for a defined population, and we suggest how writers, store owners and answer engines can cite it with its range, age and definition.

papers.title: From User Behaviors to Satisfaction Judgments: Reasoning about User Satisfaction with AI Overviews
papers.venue: arXiv
papers.abstract: The growing presence of AI overviews in everyday search makes their effective evaluation essential. Response quality has been the primary focus of existing evaluation research, with only a small number of studies examining the user perspective. These evaluations rely on queries and response content, leaving the information conveyed by user behavior insufficiently utilized. This work investigates satisfaction prediction for AI overviews from a user-centered perspective and incorporates behavioral signals into the prediction process. Applying existing behavior-based satisfaction prediction methods from traditional information retrieval to this setting, however, presents limitations. We address these limitations with STaRS, an LLM-based approach designed specifically for predicting satisfaction with AI overviews. At its core is a structured reasoning procedure: individual behavioral signals are interpreted first, and their implications then inform the prediction of user satisfaction. Reinforcement learning further optimizes this procedure, while a reward shaping mechanism alleviates reward sparsity during training. Evaluation on two real-world datasets demonstrates that STaRS outperforms the comparison methods in satisfaction prediction, providing search providers with a practical means of accurately estimating users' satisfaction with AI overviews.

papers.title: A Source-Checked Analysis of Google's Gemini Models on Long Context, Grounding, Cost, and Device Fit
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Google's Gemini model family has grown from multimodal assistants into cloud image and video generators, on-device models and tiered paid plans. This preprint is a source-checked analysis of public claims about these models. It compares vendor specifications with independent evidence in five areas. First, long-context retrieval, where single-needle recall results contrast with lower reported multi-needle scores. Second, search grounding, where studies of Google's AI Overviews find that accurate answers are often not fully supported by their citations; one analysis reports about 91% accuracy but only 39% of overviews both correct and fully supported. Third, cost per task rather than cost per token. Fourth, naming, plan and pricing changes that make it hard to know which model is in use. Fifth, device fit across Gemini Nano, Flash, Pro, Argon and the Nano Banana image models. Primary sources, including Google documentation, technical reports and an original study, are separated from secondary reports, and unverified claims are flagged. The paper ends with a practical model-selection guide and four open questions for developers and Google. It is a non-peer-reviewed analysis of public information as of November 5, 2026, and it reports no new experiments.

Audited Credit Unions suffered a 95.0% Total Brand Omission rate (5.0% visibility), while Ethical Fintechs suffered a 97.1% Total Brand Omission rate (2.9% visibility). 2. 0.0% Foundational Deposit Blackout (Q01–Q03): On the three core consumer deposit queries ($10,000 emergency fund high-yield savings, $500/month savings account, and highest 12-month CD rate for $25,000), all 12 audited Credit Unions and Fintechs recorded 0.0% visibility (0 out of 144 evaluations) across all four AI models. 3. 95.7% Cross-Engine Disagreement: Across 336 total recommendation slots (234 unique query-entity pairs), all four AI models agreed on the same financial institution only 3.8% of the time (4.3% including federal FHA mortgage programs). Over two-thirds (68.4%) of recommended institutions were named by only a single AI engine and completely omitted by the other three. 4. Megabank Collapse (5.4%) & Middleman Capture (17.3%): On specific dollar-tier and credit-score transactional prompts, the "Big 4" U.S. Megabanks captured just 5.4% of total AI recommendation slots combined. Abstract (English) How do AI search assistants answer questions about businesses that do not exist? 162 answers on nine fictional Korean businesses across three models (2026-09-14). We invented ten local business names in Busan, Korea (clinics, a law firm, a rental service, an agency, a dentist, a Korean-medicine clinic, a tax office, an academy and a cosmetics brand). Each name had no web search results. We asked three search-enabled models about each one, with a reputation question and a details question (location, prices, hours): 180 calls, no failures. One canary was excluded because cited pages contained a similar real brand. On the remaining 162 answers, GPT mostly denied knowing the business (74%). Gemini mostly recommended other, real businesses instead (80%, and 93% for detail questions). Perplexity denied in 56% of answers but presented fabricated facts such as addresses, opening hours and "verified reviews" in 15% (fabricate 9%, mixed 6%), with no citations attached. GPT and Gemini fabricated nothing. Labels come from a single LLM judge (Gemini) cross-checked with regular expressions. Raw answers, labels and the judging prompt are included.

papers.title: What AI answer engines cite when Malaysian SMEs ask for marketing help
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: When Malaysian SMEs ask an AI assistant for marketing help, who publishes the pages its answer cites? This observational audit examines source ownership in answers to 42 English-language questions across seven marketing-service categories, covering provider selection, how a service works and cost. Each question was asked of Gemini and ChatGPT through their developer APIs three times in each of two collection windows: 26–27 September and 4 October 2026. The main panel comprises 504 answers and 2,445 coded citations. Provider-owned pages accounted for 87.4% of Gemini's citations and 59.9% of ChatGPT's. For provider-selection questions, the corresponding shares were 86.1% and 84.8%, an exploratory split. A separate exploratory Bahasa Malaysia arm comprises 72 trials and 401 citations; the combined API dataset covers 576 trials and 2,846 citations. A small Google AI-answer browser sub-panel is reported separately in the paper and supporting tables. The package includes the report, protocol and deviation log, frozen prompt panel, codebook, generated tables, anonymised trial-level dataset, literature-search record and README. The public CSV supports recomputing shares by source type, publisher country and page type. Agency identities and most URL paths are withheld, so agency-level overlap and concentration cannot be independently recomputed from that CSV alone. The results describe a designed question panel and fixed API configurations on the collection dates. They do not establish causation, source quality, consumer-app performance or business outcomes. The study was produced by ALIQ Studio, which sells marketing and AI-visibility services, and received internal rather than independent peer review. Author: Yik Jinn, Head of SEO and AI Search at ALIQ Studio. Version 1.1 was released on 5 November 2026; the report was first published on 6 October 2026. The original publication and public supporting materials are available at https://studio.aliqgroup.com/en/research/ai-answer-citations-malaysia-2026/. Version note: Version 1.1 updates the discussion of Cloudflare's crawler policy to reflect the documentation re-read on 5 November 2026 and its difference from the July announcement described in v1.0. No study figure or finding changed. Version 1.0 remains available on the original website as a superseded edition.

papers.title: 2026 U.S. Commercial Banking AI Search Visibility Study: Measuring Total Brand Omission Across Megabanks and Super-Regional Banks on ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: EquiSchema AI LLC conducted a 1,200-evaluation empirical benchmark study across the four leading generative AI search platforms (OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Perplexity AI, and Anthropic Claude) to measure how often the 12 largest U.S. commercial banks (6 U.S. Megabanks and 6 U.S. Super-Regional Banks) are recommended when consumers and small business owners ask unbranded, high-intent financial questions. This baseline study introduces and quantifies Total Brand Omission—defined by EquiSchema AI as the complete exclusion of a qualified financial institution from unbranded, bottom-of-funnel borrower and depositor recommendations, leaving the institution with a 0% probability of customer consideration. KEY EMPIRICAL FINDINGS (REPORT NO. 2026-01): 1. 91.4% Aggregate Total Brand Omission (1,200 Evaluations): Across 25 high-intent retail deposit, small business lending, wealth/CD, real estate, and consumer lending queries evaluated across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude, the 12 audited commercial banks achieved just 8.6% aggregate visibility (91.4% Total Brand Omission). 2. Megabanks (11.3% Visibility) vs. Super-Regional Banks (5.8% Visibility): The 6 U.S. Megabanks suffered an 88.7% Total Brand Omission rate, while the 6 U.S. Super-Regional Banks suffered a 94.2% Total Brand Omission rate (and a 97.4% omission rate when excluding a single outlier, Super-Regional 3, which achieved 22.0% visibility via specialized SBA and physician mortgage pages). 3. 0.0% Deposit & CD Blackout: Across all 6 Super-Regional Banks, visibility on rate-driven savings, money market, and CD queries was 0.0% (100% Total Brand Omission). On $25,000 savings (Q02), $40,000 money market (Q05), $100,000 18-month CD (Q11), $250,000 IRA rollover (Q13), and $20,000 12-month CD (Q15), all 12 audited Megabanks and Super-Regionals recorded a 0.0% blackout across all four AI models. 4. Specialty Semantic Proof vs. Mainstream Erasure: Super-Regional banks achieved strong visibility on $750,000 zero-down physician mortgages (Q18) where exact dollar caps and borrower personas were explicitly stated in page text, yet suffered 0% lender inclusion on $400,000 first-time homebuyer mortgages (Q20, ceded to Fannie Mae) and $45,000 650-score truck loans (Q21, ceded to Credit Unions). papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: An Excel sheet for Google Search Console query data from two periods. It flags queries where click-through rate fell by 25% or more while average position moved by 1.0 or less (with at least 100 impressions in the later period; all three settings can be changed). The user records whether an AI Overview showed for each flagged query, and the sheet splits the lost clicks into AI Overview queries and queries with no AI Overview. Room for 500 queries. papers.title: Recommending Is Not Citing: Separable and Competing Mechanisms for Entity Mention and Source Attribution in Large Language Models
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: When a language model answers a question from numbered sources, two outputs that are often treated as one can come apart: whether it names an entity (recommends a brand) and whether it cites the source that supports that entity. We study this split in a controlled retrieval-augmented setting: five numbered sources, one per brand, a purchase question, and an explicit instruction to cite with bracketed numbers. The target brand's source sits at position [3] and is either neutral or carries one concrete fact. We read next-token probabilities in five open-weight models (Qwen3.5 4B, 27B, 122B-A10B, 397B-A17B-FP8 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash) and generated text in two API models (GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash). In every model, the concrete fact raises the probability of naming the brand (e.g. 1.7% to 47.7% in the 27B; 1.8% to 44.4% in the 397B) and lowers the probability of citing that same source once the brand is named (5.9% to 3.2%; 11.2% to 2.3%). In the API models the citation drop appears only under the citation instruction. Internally, difference-of-means directions for "recommend" and "cite" are nearly orthogonal at the positions where each decision is made (mean |cosine| 0.03–0.09, against split-half noise ceilings an order of magnitude higher) and partially anti-aligned at the position right after the brand. Adding the "recommend" direction raises naming and lowers citation beyond a random-direction control in three models. Activation patching places the citation decision in the last ~10% of depth, after the naming decision in the 27B and 397B. With sparse autoencoders on the 27B, ablating about ten features cuts the fact-driven recommendation from 70% to 32% (random ablation: 68%), whereas the late-layer features tied to citation look like reference-formatting features; we found no feature resembling "this claim needs support". Attention analysis splits citing into whether to open a bracket and which index to write: the index is correct 99% of the time and is computed redundantly (ablating up to 32 attention heads matches random ablation), while the fact acts on whether. A short observational sample of Google AI Overviews in Argentina is consistent with mention and attribution being separate in production. We conclude that entity mention and source attribution should be measured and studied as separate behaviours.

papers.title: AI Search Visibility Research Report Cover
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Search is evolving beyond traditional lists of web pages. AI-powered experiences such as Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode and Microsoft Copilot are changing how people discover information, compare options and explore businesses. For website owners, this creates an important challenge: making useful information accessible, understandable and reliable across different search experiences. This report presents a practical framework for improving website visibility in AI-assisted search. It examines technical accessibility, content quality, information structure, entity clarity, structured data and performance measurement. It also explains how traditional Search Engine Optimization (SEO), Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) and Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) relate to one another. The framework is based on publicly available search platform documentation and established website optimization practices. It does not claim that any specific technique guarantees inclusion in AI-generated answers, citations or search results. Keywords: AI Search, AI SEO, Search Engine Optimization, Answer Engine Optimization, Generative Engine Optimization, Website Visibility, Technical SEO, Content Quality. 1. Introduction People increasingly use AI-powered search experiences to explore topics, understand complex questions and compare products or services. Instead of relying exclusively on traditional search results, users may receive summarized answers with links to supporting websites. These changes do not make traditional SEO irrelevant. Search platforms still depend on processes such as discovering, crawling, indexing and evaluating online content. Google explains that its AI search features use its existing search foundations and that established SEO practices remain relevant. The practical objective for website owners is therefore not to chase individual AI ranking tricks. It is to build websites that provide useful information, maintain technical accessibility and communicate their subject matter clearly. 2. Understanding SEO, AEO and GEO These terms describe related approaches to improving the discoverability and usefulness of online information. 2.1 Search Engine Optimization (SEO) SEO focuses on improving a website's ability to be discovered and understood through search engines. It includes technical accessibility, relevant content, site structure, internal linking and other established practices. 2.2 Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) AEO focuses on making information easy to identify and understand when users search for direct answers. Clear explanations, descriptive headings and well-organized information can improve usability and help systems interpret a page. 2.3 Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) GEO refers to improving the clarity, relevance and credibility of content for generative AI-powered discovery experiences. It emphasizes useful information, clear context and reliable supporting sources. These approaches overlap. They should be treated as complementary parts of a broader digital visibility strategy rather than completely separate disciplines. 3. Build a Technically Accessible Website High-quality content cannot deliver its full discovery potential if search systems cannot access or process the website properly. Website owners should review the following areas: Crawlability: Ensure that important pages are not unintentionally blocked by robots.txt, hosting configurations or other access restrictions. Indexability: Check that valuable pages can be indexed and are not affected by unintended noindex directives. Internal linking: Connect related pages through descriptive links so users and search systems can discover important content. XML sitemap: Maintain an accurate sitemap containing relevant canonical URLs. Mobile experience: Ensure that important content and navigation work across mobile and desktop devices. Page performance: Reduce unnecessary scripts, oversized assets and other elements that negatively affect usability. JavaScript rendering: Confirm that important content is accessible when the website relies on JavaScript. Google's documentation states that pages must meet its existing Search technical requirements to be eligible for supporting links in AI search features. Eligibility, however, does not guarantee crawling, indexing or display. 4. Create Helpful and Distinctive Content Content quality is central to long-term search visibility. Publishing large quantities of similar articles does not automatically establish authority or usefulness. A strong content strategy should prioritize: 4.1 Answer Real User Questions Understand what the intended audience wants to learn, compare or accomplish. Develop content around genuine search needs rather than producing pages solely to target keyword variations. 4.2 Provide Meaningful Information Explain concepts with sufficient detail. Include relevant examples, practical considerations and useful context instead of repeating common statements. 4.3 Demonstrate First-Hand Knowledge Where possible, include original observations, professional experience, real project details and verified examples. Clearly distinguish direct experience from general recommendations. 4.4 Use Clear Language Write in a natural and direct style. Define technical terminology when necessary and organize longer explanations into logical sections. 4.5 Keep Information Accurate Review facts, statistics, product information and external references before publication. Update content when information becomes outdated. Google's guidance emphasizes original, helpful and people-first content rather than pages created primarily to manipulate search rankings. 5. Improve Content Structure and Context A well-organized page makes information easier for readers to navigate and understand. Consider these practices: Use descriptive headings that accurately represent each section. Keep paragraphs focused on one main idea. Explain important terms before relying on them throughout an article. Use lists or tables when they make comparisons easier. Add relevant examples to clarify complex information. Include dates where freshness is important. Link to reliable sources when supporting factual statements. Avoid unnecessary repetition and keyword stuffing. There is no need to divide every article into extremely small sections or force a question-and-answer format. The structure should serve the reader and reflect the complexity of the subject. 6. Establish Clear Business and Entity Information A website should communicate who operates it, what it offers and which audience it serves. Businesses can improve this clarity by maintaining consistent information across their website and relevant public profiles. Important elements include: A clear About page describing the organization. Accurate business name and contact information. Specific descriptions of products and services. Consistent information across relevant business profiles. Author information where professional attribution is appropriate. Verifiable credentials, qualifications and project information. Clear distinctions between the business, its employees and its services. These details help visitors understand the organization and evaluate whether its information is relevant to their needs. Businesses should never invent credentials, reviews, partnerships or experience to appear more authoritative. 7. Use Structured Data Carefully Structured data provides search engines with additional information about the content of a page. Depending on the website, relevant schema types may include: Organization LocalBusiness Article BreadcrumbList Product Service The appropriate markup depends on the actual content and Google's eligibility guidelines. Structured data should accurately represent information visible on the page. It should not contain fabricated reviews, unsupported claims or misleading business details. Importantly, structured data is not a guaranteed method of appearing in AI-generated answers. Google states that no special schema markup is required for its AI Overviews or AI Mode. 8. Develop a Relevant Internal Linking Structure Internal links connect related information and help visitors explore a website. A useful internal linking strategy should: Connect service pages with relevant educational resources. Link supporting articles to broader topic pages. Use descriptive anchor text that explains the destination. Ensure important pages are reachable through normal navigation or contextual links. Avoid excessive links that interrupt the reading experience. For example, an article explaining technical website accessibility can link to a detailed technical SEO resource. A guide about online discovery can link to relevant pages about SEO and AI search. Links should be added because they provide useful context, not simply to increase the number of internal links. 9. Measure Visibility and Website Performance AI search visibility is not a single metric. Website owners should evaluate several indicators to understand whether their content is reaching the intended audience. Useful measurement areas include: Measurement area What to review Organic search Impressions, clicks and search queries Indexing Indexed pages and technical issues Website engagement Relevant visits and user interactions Conversions Form submissions, calls and enquiries Content performance Pages attracting relevant visitors Referral traffic Visits from identifiable external sources AI search presence Available citations, mentions and referral visits Google Search Console can help monitor search performance and technical indexing information. Website analytics tools can provide additional context about visitor behaviour and conversions. Where possible

papers.title: Answering the fan-out does not predict AI Overview citation: a pre-registered test across 235 queries
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI search systems answer a question by running several related searches, a technique Google calls query fan-out. A market of tools now scores pages by how many of these sub-queries they answer, on the premise that coverage raises the chance of being cited. This study tested that premise with a pre-registered observational design. The sample was 235 non-branded keywords for which a page from one of 46 domains had been cited in a Google AI Overview. Candidate pages were the organic top ten plus every cited page. Fan-out was observed directly from Gemini with Google Search grounding (705 calls) and Claude with web search (470 calls), and guessed by a model asked to predict it (470 calls). Results pages were collected for 539 sub-queries. In conditional logistic regression within each query (158 test queries, 1,190 pages, 670 cited), a better organic rank for the head query was strongly associated with citation (odds ratio 0.43 per standard deviation of log rank) and longer pages were cited more (1.30). Heading similarity to the query, ranking in the top ten for a sub-query, and the share of sub-queries a page answers added no out-of-sample discrimination (change in within-query AUC from minus 0.003 to plus 0.004, against a pre-set bar of plus 0.02), and guessed sub-queries did as well as observed ones. Observed fan-out was small: 2.35 clusters of sub-queries per keyword against 16.1 guessed, and Gemini ran no search at all in 47% of its answers. Of cited pages outside the head query's top ten, 14% ranked in the top ten for any observed sub-query. A same-day replication on a second data provider agreed. Fan-out coverage scores are not supported as predictors of AI Overview citation; rank for the head query and length are.

papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: A fact-checked snapshot of what three AI search tools told UK university applicants in October 2026. On 20 and 21 October 2026, 21 applicant-style questions about UK universities (entry grades, fees, league-table positions, graduate outcomes, contextual offers and "which is better" comparisons) were put to ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews: 63 answers in total. Every specific, checkable claim in those answers (198 claims) was checked against the university's own pages or official data (DfE, HESA, Discover Uni, UCAS), and given one of five outcomes: Correct, Wrong, Outdated, Overstated or Unverifiable. Headline results: 125 of 198 claims (63%) were correct, and 48 (24%) were wrong, out of date or overstated. ChatGPT was correct on 72% of its claims, Perplexity on 61% and Google AI Overviews on 55%. Accuracy depended more on the source an answer drew on than on the platform: answers drawn from a university's current official page were right 79% of the time, against 7% for answers drawn from out-of-date pages on the university's own website. The dataset also includes an audit of the rankings pages of all 31 universities in the study set (the 24 Russell Group members plus Bath, Dundee, Lancaster, Loughborough, St Andrews, Strathclyde and Surrey), recording which league-table editions each page showed, with every row backed by a dated PDF or screenshot. Pilot runs using open "which universities should I apply to?" questions are published separately (pilot_claims.csv, pilot_runs.csv) and are not included in the headline figures. They show ChatGPT tailoring university shortlists to the user's approximate location, signed in and signed out. We logged 1,160 answers from ChatGPT (search), Perplexity, Gemini (Google Search grounding) and Google AI Overviews to a fixed panel of 33 buyer prompts in 19 categories, across 26 run dates from 1 July to 31 October 2026. papers.title: How Google AI Overviews Select & Cite Sources: Query Fan-Out, Conversational Prompts & Passage Extraction (400-Query Commercial SERP Dataset & Industry Synthesis)
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Summary Open dataset on Google AI Overviews and AI Mode: of 1,116 top-three organic results across 372 US searches, 80.5% were not among the first three AI citations. The audit covered 400 US searches in four commercial sectors, and 372 of them showed an AI answer. In 200 of those 372 (53.8%), none of the top three organic pages was cited. The deposit includes a 12-slide research briefing (PDF) and the two CSV files behind it. The full web study, a 15-slide practitioner checkmap, and a short video walkthrough are linked at the end. How Google’s AI answers find their sources People now type longer, more specific questions and can ask follow-ups inside Google’s AI answers. Google Search Central’s documentation on AI features says AI Overviews and AI Mode can use a technique called query fan-out, which runs several related searches at once and draws supporting pages from across them. In practice, a page can rank first for a short keyword and still be passed over when someone asks about a price, a symptom, or a standard that the page does not state clearly. Our working model This is a simplified model we used to organize the audit. It is not Google’s official pipeline. The searcher’s question is split into sub-questions: definition, price, specifications, symptoms, standards, comparisons. Related searches run for each sub-question. Passages that answer a sub-question cleanly, such as a short answer, a table, or a numbered list, are easier to quote than long narrative sections. Off-site signals such as YouTube videos and third-party mentions may help confirm who is behind the content. What other studies report Semrush’s 2026 study of 600,000+ SERPs reports AI Overviews on 88% of commercial evaluation searches, up 71% across commercial queries. Pew Research Center found people clicked a traditional result in 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, compared with 15% when it did not. Ahrefs found that the average click-through rate of the top-ranking page was 58% lower on keywords with an AI Overview (December 2025 data, 300,000 keywords). This is a correlation, not a controlled test. Seer Interactive reports that brands cited in an AI Overview earned 35% more organic clicks and 91% more paid clicks than uncited brands on the same results. This is an observed difference, not a controlled test. Aggarwal et al. (ACM SIGKDD 2024) found in their generative-engine benchmark that adding statistics, authoritative citations, and quotations improved source visibility, while keyword stuffing did not. They did not test Google AI Overviews directly. Ahrefs’ 75,000-brand study found that YouTube mentions (0.737), digital PR mentions (0.664), and branded anchors (0.527) correlated more strongly with AI visibility than backlink volume did (0.218). These are correlations. What we found in the 400-query audit Scope We ran 400 US queries, 100 each in Local Home Services, E-Commerce and Retail, B2B Commercial and Industrial, and SaaS and Enterprise Software. For each query we recorded the top three organic results and the first three AI citation cards. 372 queries (93.0%) showed an AI answer and 28 (7.0%) did not. Of the 372 answers, 215 were standard AI Overviews and 157 were AI Mode responses. Organic rank versus AI citations Across 1,116 top-three organic slots, 182 (16.3%) were cited with the exact same page, 36 (3.2%) were cited through a companion guide on the same domain, and 898 (80.5%) were not cited among the first three cards. Organic position Exact page cited Companion guide cited Not cited #1 (372 slots) 70 (18.8%) 16 (4.3%) 286 (76.9%) #2 (372 slots) 63 (16.9%) 8 (2.2%) 301 (80.9%) #3 (372 slots) 49 (13.2%) 12 (3.2%) 311 (83.6%) All (1,116 slots) 182 (16.3%) 36 (3.2%) 898 (80.5%) At the query level, 200 queries (53.8%) cited none of the top three organic pages, 129 (34.7%) cited one, 40 (10.8%) cited two, and 3 (0.8%) cited all three. Results by sector Sector Queries with an AI answer Top-3 slots Exact page Companion guide Combined Local Home Services 86 of 100 258 45 6 51 (19.8%) E-Commerce and Retail 99 of 100 297 40 20 60 (20.2%) B2B Commercial and Industrial 87 of 100 261 54 8 62 (23.8%) SaaS and Enterprise Software 100 of 100 300 43 2 45 (15.0%) In e-commerce, 257 of 297 category or product slots (86.5%) were not cited directly, and another 20 slots were cited through a companion buying guide on the same site. B2B had the highest combined rate and SaaS the lowest. Examples from the files: for “net revenue retention formula”, Stripe was cited while the first organic result, Klipfolio, was not. For “mattress firmness guide”, NapLab was cited while Mattress Mill ranked first. For “what is ltl freight”, Old Dominion Freight Line was cited while GoComet ranked first. For “why is my ac blowing warm”, Airflow Designs was cited while Valiant Energy ranked first. Who got cited The first three AI cards produced 1,100 citation URLs across 850 unique domains, about 1.29 citations per domain. Sixteen citation slots had no URL because some answers showed fewer than three cards. YouTube accounted for 82 of the citations. We labeled the main structure of each of the 1,100 cited pages by hand, one primary label per page: Primary format of the cited page Citations Share Direct short answer under a question heading (about 40 to 60 words) 353 32.1% HTML pricing or specification table 299 27.2% Ordered symptom-to-action checklist 185 16.8% Timestamped video (including 82 YouTube citations) 132 12.0% Named official standards or benchmarks 131 11.9% These labels are our own classification. They are not a column in the CSV files. How we read these patterns Cited pages tended to state a number, a rule, or a step plainly in one self-contained block. We treat that as a practical guide for writing pages, not as proof that any one format causes a citation. The full playbook is in the web study linked below. Putting these patterns into practice usually means working on three layers together: page structure, entity and trust signals, and off-site mentions. Our overview of that work is on the AI search optimization page. Scope and limitations This is an observational snapshot of US English searches from one collection period. AI answers change often. We recorded only the first three citation cards. Some AI answers show more sources. The audit describes what cited pages looked like. It does not test whether adding those formats to a page causes a citation. The “Why Ranked” and “Why Cited” columns in the CSV files are analyst notes and are best read as hypotheses. Dataset guide File 1: SERP Analysis 2026 - SERP.csv 1,200 rows and 10 columns: the top three organic results (Pos #1 to #3) for each of the 400 queries. Target Keyword, Industry, and AI Overview Triggered? appear on the first row of each three-row block. Column I, Cited in AI Overview?, uses three kinds of values: YES (Citation #1, #2, or #3) for the exact page (182 slots), YES (Citation #1, #2, or #3 — Domain Cluster) for a companion page on the same domain (36 slots), and NO (Organic Only) (898 slots). The 28 queries without an AI answer account for the remaining 84 rows. File 2: SERP Analysis 2026 - Google AI Overview.csv 1,200 rows and 10 columns: Citation #1, #2, and #3 for each query, with the AI answer text (column D), cited brand (F), cited URL (G), in-text anchor (H), page structure (I), and analyst rationale (J). It holds 1,100 cited URLs across 850 unique domains. Sixteen slots in answers with fewer than three cards, and the 84 slots for queries without an AI answer, have no URL. How to reproduce the counts The counts of citations, skipped slots, sectors, and domains can be reproduced by filtering these two files. The format shares in the table above come from hand labeling. papers.title: Does the Citation Matter? Quality, Grounding, and Physician-Rubric Accuracy of Google's AI Overviews for Medical Information
papers.venue: arXiv
papers.abstract: Google's AI Overviews (AIOs) are the first result users encounter when searching the web, shifting the work of selecting and evaluating sources from the user to Gemini. This may be especially consequential for health information, given that Google's traditional algorithm was designed to prioritize quality sources, and inaccurate information carries health risks. We evaluated 3,611 benchmark health questions, comparing each AIO against that question's top five traditional results on source selection and quality. We also evaluated the AIOs' statement grounding in their cited sources and how accurate AIOs were against physician-written rubrics. Overviews appeared for 96.4% of questions but drew on substantially different evidence than traditional search: only 44.4% of the top five results were cited by the corresponding AIO, which instead overrepresented commercial health publishers (e.g., WebMD, Healthline) at the expense of academic and government sources (e.g., Cleveland Clinic, National Health Service). AIO-cited pages scored lower than traditional results on four of six well-established credibility criteria. The grounding of AIO statements to their sources was poor: after correcting for classifier error, an estimated 56.7% of cited statements were supported by their cited page, and a further 20.8% of all statements were factual claims with no citation at all. When AIOs were graded against physicians' rubrics, they earned 38.2% of all available points (e.g., accuracy 54.2%, completeness 21.6%), and among the subset of AIOs whose physician rubric anticipated a specific inaccurate or potentially harmful claim, 22.2% of AIOs contained the harmful content. Notably, the accuracy of AIOs was unrelated to the grounding of their statements. We recommend AIO literacy interventions for users and holding AIOs at least to Google's own health-ranking standards.

papers.title: Who Owns Digital News, and Who Gets Cited: Measuring Media Concentration Across 77 Countries and Seven AI Systems
papers.venue: arXiv
papers.abstract: Digital news outlets compete for audience attention. Search engines equipped with generative AI systems such as Google's AI overviews increasingly decide where that attention goes, as well as the revenue it represents. Yet, the lack of a consistent data collection infrastructure between national-level regulatory bodies has hindered between-country comparative analysis of media concentration, and with it any assessment of how these intermediaries reshape digital news markets. To address this issue, we compile an ownership dataset for 9,761 digital news outlets drawn from Wikipedia and Wikidata, achieving high agreement with independently compiled US and UK news directories. Using this dataset, we derive traffic-weighted concentration indices for 77 countries. We find that journalists report more owner pressure in countries with higher concentration, and that outlet-level measures understate concentration, with owner-level indices a median 1.30x higher. Applying concentration measures to AI-mediated news discovery, we find that citation distributions from major AI systems are up to 2.08x more concentrated than traffic, and that if Google AI Overviews mediated all organic search, the resulting rise in US concentration would be several times that associated with highly regulated media mergers and acquisitions. Finally, our analyses indicate that AI systems preferentially cite state-controlled media outlets when prompted in that country's native language. Together, these findings raise concerns about the effect AI systems may have on digital media. We release the dataset to enable the monitoring of digital news globally, so that the impact of disruptive technologies on digital media markets can be tracked as they emerge.

papers.title: Auditer la citabilité d'une marque par les IA génératives : la méthode NEXUS GEO et le Référentiel GEO-47
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Résumé. Le generative engine optimization (GEO) désigne le travail qui vise à faire citer une marque, avec des informations exactes, dans les réponses rédigées par les IA génératives. Cette note décrit la méthode d’audit et d’accompagnement de NEXUS GEO, telle qu’elle est publiée sur son site. L’audit évalue un site et sa présence en ligne selon le Référentiel GEO-47 : 8 piliers, 47 critères, un score global sur 100. Sa grille vaut pour toutes les IA ; la mesure de la présence de la marque porte sur cinq IA (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Mistral et Google AI Overviews), face à trois concurrents nommés. La note présente les trois étapes de la méthode, les indicateurs, les livrables, ce qui est publié et ce qui ne l’est pas, et les limites de la démarche. Abstract. Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the work of getting a brand cited, with accurate information, in answers written by generative AI assistants. This note describes the audit and support method of NEXUS GEO, a French agency, as published on its website. The audit assesses a website and its online presence against the GEO-47 Framework: 8 pillars, 47 criteria and an overall score out of 100. The assessment grid applies to all AI assistants; the brand’s presence is measured on five of them (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Mistral and Google AI Overviews), against three named competitors. The note sets out the three stages of the method, its indicators and deliverables, what is published and what is not, and the method’s limits. Version en ligne, tenue à jour / Online version: https://nexus-geo.fr/methodologie ; Référentiel GEO-47 : https://nexus-geo.fr/referentiel-geo-47

papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This record is a copy for citation. The canonical dataset and its write-up are at https://appeareverywhere.com/guides/what-the-ai-assistants-cite/, and the canonical CSV at https://appeareverywhere.com/guides/what-the-ai-assistants-cite/data.csv. papers.title: Brands ranked in the top three positions by AI engines in October 2026 had faster branded search growth from ChatGPT's launch in 2022 than brands outside the top three positions: exploratory evidence from 418 US brands
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Ranking Atlas Working Paper RA-WP-2026-03. Not peer reviewed. Background. When people ask an AI engine which product to buy or which service to use, it answers with a short list of brands in order. Practitioners describe this as a branding channel: people meet a brand in an AI answer, then search for it by name on Google. If position in these lists is linked to later searches, brands placed near the top should show faster growth in branded search. Our earlier study of 347 US brands found that brands ChatGPT and Gemini recommended grew about 7 pp per year faster in Google Ads searches than matched brands, but the result was unstable over time (Grainger, 2026). Methods. We measured recommendation position again with five engines (ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode, Google AI Overviews and Perplexity) and 280 brand-free category prompts, run six times each on 23-24 October 2026 (8,190 answers). Each of 418 US brands was placed in a band: position 1, positions 2-3, position 4 or later, or not named. We compared these bands with each brand's Google Ads search volume growth from October 2022 to September 2026, a window that begins two months before ChatGPT's public launch on 30 November 2022, which we treat as the start of mainstream AI engine use. Google Trends was a second source, and 2015-2022, before ChatGPT, a placebo period. Growth is reported in pp of annual growth (100 x the yearly change in ln volume; 1 pp is roughly 1% per year). Positions are a single October 2026 snapshot compared retrospectively with earlier growth; past AI answers cannot be reconstructed. Results. The 68 brands placed in the top three grew 8.2 pp per year (about 8.5% a year) faster than the other 350, after controlling for category and starting volume (95% CI 3.3 to 13.2). Google Trends gave a similar estimate (+7.9; 95% CI 1.7 to 14.1). In 2015-2022, before ChatGPT's launch, no growth advantage was detected (-1.6; 95% CI -5.3 to 2.1). The gap appeared in both halves of the post-ChatGPT period in Ads (+11.1 and +7.4). None of the pre-specified tests was supported: brands at position 1 and at positions 2-3 grew at similar rates, and the rank-ordering test was not significant after Holm correction. In post hoc checks, the gap was similar when compared with brands of the same starting volume (7.6 to 8.7 pp), and 10 of 12 randomly drawn top-3 brands grew faster than their category median. Conclusions. Brands that AI engines place in the top three have grown faster in branded search since ChatGPT's public launch, on two data sources and in both halves of the period, with no detectable gap before ChatGPT. The comparison was chosen after the data were seen, so the result is an association, not evidence that AI ranking causes search growth. A prospective study that measures position first will be preregistered publicly.

papers.title: A closed loop multimodal auditing framework for enhancing artificial intelligence reliability in medical emergency response
papers.venue: Discover Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Ensuring the reliability of AI-powered information retrieval systems is critical in high-stakes domains such as first aid. Traditional audit methodologies are often static, manual, and unimodal, failing to address the dynamic, time-sensitive, and multimodal requirements of these applications. To overcome these limitations, we introduce RADAR-FirstAid (Reliability-Aware Dynamic Auditing Framework), a closed-loop auditing pipeline — not a competing information system — for real-time, multimodal, and edge-aware auditing. Its key components include a Dynamic Query Simulator for generating criticality-weighted scenarios, a Multimodal Audit & Fusion Agent for verifying cross-modal consistency, a Differentiable Reliability Evaluator that employs LLM-based judges for automated assessment, and an Edge-Optimization Scheduler for efficient deployment. Applying the framework to a curated dataset of 1, 508 first-aid queries, we conduct a large-scale audit of Google’s AI Overviews (AIO) and Featured Snippets (FS), operated purely as black-box Systems under Audit. The audit reveals substantial reliability gaps: automated consistency scores of $$\Phi _{cons}=0.68$$ (FS) and 0.72 (AIO), safety/relevance scores of $$\Phi _{safe}=0.71$$ (FS) and 0.76 (AIO), and pronounced weaknesses on safety-critical “Binary” and “How-to” queries and on negative-sentiment queries where cautious tone matters most. Manual annotation on a 200-query subset validates the automated evaluation (Spearman $$\rho = 0.74$$ –0.87). Ablation studies confirm the essential role of each pipeline module, and geographical variance is minimal (SD $$<0.03$$ ). RADAR-FirstAid offers a scalable, automated, and reproducible audit instrument for AI-powered search systems in safety-critical domains.

Sites with both average 93.6 out of 100; sites with neither average 48.0 (a correlation, not a causal effect). - Average AI visibility score 79.2, median 85. What is AI visibility? papers.title: From Search Engines to AI Answers: The New Rules of SEO, GEO, and Digital Marketing
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Search has shifted from ranked lists of blue links to AI answers. In 2026, industry keyword trackers report Google AI Overviews shown on roughly 43–50% of queries, while the one large-scale academic measurement study reviewed here finds substantially lower overall activation (13.7%, rising to 64.7% for question-form queries), a gap this article attributes to differences between commercial tracking samples and broad academic query samples rather than treating either figure as settled; coverage is markedly higher for informational and decision-related queries in both types of study. Zero-click rates vary from 37% for transactional queries to 92% for informational queries (aggregating to roughly 75% overall), and rise from 63% without an AI Overview present to 82% when one is; citation overlap with traditional Google rankings sits as low as 14–17% in several studies. Standing number one is no longer enough. This article explores the new rules of visibility in the generative age. Operating on up-to-date signals from BrightEdge, SparkToro, Similarweb, First Page Sage, Pew, Ahrefs, Princeton GEO research, Google Search Console generative reports along with the author’s practical track record of scaling SEO- and GEO-based Answer Engine Optimisation (AEO) systems, it lays out the continuum of SEO, GEO and Answer Engine Optimisation (AEO), offers seven evidence-based rules centred on entity clarity (mainly Wikipedia and Wikidata), citability signals (statistics, source citations, expert quotations), third-party corroboration, technical eligibility, multi-engine strategy, evolved measurement, and content freshness, and concludes with an operational implementation pathway and strategic implications for digital marketing teams. Brands that choose to see SEO and GEO as a single seamless system of authority and discoverability will monopolise the next decade of digital visibility; those that do not will gradually lose category presence within the answers users now receive.

papers.title: What Is Associated with Being Cited in AI Answers? Page, Domain and Query Features on Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode, Perplexity and Yandex Alice, Russian-Language Queries, October 2026
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Search-optimisation advice for AI answers lists dozens of ranking factors, most of them taken from vendor studies that differ in data, platform and method. This preprint compares 38 of them with one snapshot of Russian-language results. The main collection covers 2400 queries in 16 niches on Google AI Overviews (88230 result pages at organic positions 1–50, 2045 queries with a block that has links) and 800 queries on Yandex Alice (368 blocks with links). Smaller collections add Google AI Mode (181 queries with links), Perplexity Sonar (45 queries) and 303 brand queries per engine. The outcome is whether a result page is a link of the AI block. Each feature is fitted in a logit model with the organic position (and, for text and structure features, page length) as controls, two-way clustered standard errors and a Benjamini–Hochberg correction within each platform. Organic position matters most on Google: a page at rank 1 is a link of the block with probability 65.1%, at rank 10 with 16.1%, at rank 20 with 2.4%. Yandex Alice behaves differently: 23.9% of its links stand in the organic top 10 and 63.9% are absent from the top 50 of the same query. At equal position, informational pages are cited more often than commercial ones, and the semantic closeness of the title to the query has a positive sign on all four platforms (odds ratio 1.26 per standard deviation on Google). Domain-authority measures show no positive association on Google. A stated author is associated with citation on Google (1.23) and AI Mode (1.77) and borderline on Perplexity; Article markup on Google (1.30) and Perplexity (3.03). Point estimates are higher on the two small-sample platforms, but their intervals overlap with Google's. A within-query sensitivity analysis with query fixed effects keeps the direction of all selected estimates; two of them lose significance. The record contains the preprint (PDF) and a replication package: model-ready tables without commercial metrics, links of the AI blocks, the results of every fit, and code that refits 463 models (largest deviation from the released estimates below 0.0001). Raw HTML, page texts, texts of AI answers and commercial domain metrics (Keys.so, Ahrefs) are not included. Text, figures and data: CC BY 4.0; code: MIT. Observational design, one date, Moscow for Google and Yandex, desktop; no causal claims. The author offers search-optimisation services and runs the AI-text detector used in one analysis (see the preprint, Competing interests). papers.title: Who Does Google Cite for Health? Auditing the Source Ecosystem of AI Overviews in Taiwan
papers.venue: ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries
papers.abstract: Google’s AI Overviews (AIO) now synthesize answers atop the search results page for a large fraction of health queries, displacing the ranked list of links that long mediated public access to health information. This represents a new venue for users to get information; however, almost all scrutiny of AIO concerns English-language, U.S.-localized search. We present the first systematic audit, to our knowledge, of the AIO source ecosystem in a non-English, non-Western setting: Traditional-Chinese (zh-TW) health search in Taiwan. Drawing on the 625 most-searched real-world Google Taiwan health queries of 2025, we characterize which sources Google elevates across the 417 overviews they triggered, and how those sources relate. Data collection was repeated over four runs to control for AIO’s instability. Each overview presents a dense citation slate (median 10 URLs, 8 hosts), often with an image (59%) but rarely a query-specific medical warning (16%). Citations are overwhelmingly Taiwan-based (90%) and dominated by healthcare providers (40%) and commercial sites (24%); academic, Wikipedia, and social media sources are each marginal (2%). The pool is long-tailed and unconcentrated (HHI ≈ 55), yet co-citation analysis of the 975 domains reveals a single hub-dominated component anchored by hospital and government portals, with Facebook and Wikipedia among the most-cited domains. We discuss implications for source transparency, AI-generated content curation, and cross-lingual algorithmic accountability.

papers.title: What Drives AI Citations? Content, Retrieval and Model Knowledge in Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)
papers.venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
papers.abstract: Generative search engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity now decide which Web pages users see as sources, and a growing industry of generative engine optimization advises publishers on how to earn these citations. We study what shapes citation in two 90-day collections of answers to commercial questions in contrasting markets: 158,099 answers with 468,037 citations. Comparing pages of the same website, content matters in one way: pages whose title and paragraphs match the questions people ask are cited more, whereas FAQ blocks, structured data, summary boxes and page speed appear effective only across websites. Page properties nevertheless explain little of the variation between pages of a website. Replaying the questions through the engines' APIs shows why. Every page ChatGPT cites is one its own search retrieved, and which pages that search retrieves, for sub-queries the model rewrites on every answer and that rarely coincide with Google's or Bing's results, explains far more of the variation than page properties (32% against 2.8%). Content acts mainly through this step, by matching the engine's queries in meaning. The model's own knowledge shapes it too: ChatGPT writes brands it knows into its searches, prefers websites it knows, and names brands without any supporting page, and controlled experiments show that brand names reorder its rankings of products with identical facts. Pages are thus cited when searched; brands are also named when remembered. The findings replicate in a market of small B2B vendors. We release data and code.

papers.title: From Web Search to AI Search: A Comparative Analysis of Information-Seeking Behaviour in Traditional Search Engines and Conversational Systems Based on Large Language Models
papers.venue: European Scientific Journal ESJ
papers.abstract: AI search is changing how users seek information: instead of typing keywords and clicking through links, users increasingly ask complex questions and obtain direct answers on the results page. This shift, together with the rise of “zero-click search” and of chatbots based on Large Language Models (LLMs), is reshaping the customer experience of information seeking. This paper examines how LLM-based search systems are changing the way users retrieve information online, moving the dominant paradigm from keyword queries and ranked lists of links to direct answers in natural language. The study offers a structured, non-systematic narrative review comparing traditional search engines (represented by Google Search) and conversational AI tools (represented by ChatGPT and GPT-3/3.5-based search tools). It synthesises eight independent studies published between 2023 and 2026: three randomised controlled experiments, two large-scale observational analyses of real-world behaviour and three studies measuring content reliability, complemented by an industry benchmark (Vectara Hallucination Leaderboard). The analysis focuses on five key performance indicators (KPIs): number of queries per task (KPI 1), task success rate/accuracy (KPI 2), total time to task completion (KPI 3), rate of consultation of external sources/outbound clicks as a proxy for cross-verification (KPI 4), and the hallucination rate of AI systems compared with the rate of unreliable results in traditional search (KPI 5). AI systems consistently reduce task completion time, whereas the reduction in the number of queries depends on the task. Accuracy improves only when the generated output is correct; when it is wrong, accuracy drops sharply, consistent with a markedly lower consultation of external sources. The risk of error exists in both paradigms under specific conditions of use. The five KPIs should therefore be read as an interdependent system, with implications for the design of hybrid search tools in human-computer interaction and information retrieval.

papers.venue: Osong Public Health and Research Perspectives
papers.abstract: Objectives: This study assessed changes in the visibility of the National Health Information Portal (NHIP), operated by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, across conventional search portals and generative artificial intelligence (AI) platforms. Methods: We analyzed 150 health-related keywords derived from NHIP traffic data, Daum search logs, and chronic disease categories across 7 platforms: Naver, Google, Bing, Daum, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini. Searches were conducted in September 2025 and February 2026; Gemini was assessed only in the second survey. NHIP exposure was defined as appearance within the top 10 organic search results, whereas AI citation was defined as explicit source attribution. Changes were tested using McNemar's test. Results: Organic search exposure for the NHIP increased on Naver (64.0% to 73.3%, p=0.018) and decreased on Bing (72.0% to 61.3%, p=0.021). AI-summary citation rates increased more substantially on Naver AI Briefing (8.0% to 62.7%, p<0.001), Bing AI Summary (6.7% to 44.7%, p<0.001), Google AI Overview (30.0% to 48.0%, p=0.001), and ChatGPT (16.7% to 38.0%, p<0.001). Gemini cited the NHIP for 96.0% of keywords. For dyslipidemia-related keywords (n=10), Google and ChatGPT showed no NHIP exposure, whereas Gemini cited the NHIP for all keywords. Conclusion: AI citation represents a new dimension of health information accessibility. To address visibility gaps and marked platform divergence, public health portals should implement a 3-level optimization strategy encompassing machine-readable infrastructure, AI-friendly content formatting, and continuous multi-platform monitoring.

The study asks whether a reader who follows an AI answer engine's own sources can find there the figures the answer gives: do the numbers in AI answers have sources? It measures whether a figure in an answer occurs on the pages that answer cites, and it does not measure whether any figure is correct. Fifty buyer questions about prices, costs, fees and value, drawn by a written rule from Google autocomplete suggestions, were put to Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT and Gemini through their free public web interfaces from a New York network exit on 5 to 7 October 2026, by fixed scripts, and the first ten were asked a second time. Two engines were added after the registration and outside it, as exploratory additions. The same fifty questions were put once to Perplexity, through a signed-in free account, and to Claude through the Anthropic API with its web search tool; the tables write Claude (API). Their answers were collected for an analysis the registration does not contain, of which sources the engines cite and how far they share them, and were then put through the registered figure chain: the same extraction, check, classifier and summary. By the instruction recorded as entry 7 of the deviation log, the result texts and the tables show the five engines together: 249 of 250 answers, 241 of them with at least one figure, 3,465 figures. The text of the cited pages and the saved answer pages are not redistributed: the record gives their addresses, fetch times and SHA-256 hashes, and quotes of at most 200 characters. papers.title: From search results to generative answers: A mixed-methods study of credibility assessment and trust formation in AI Overviews
papers.venue: Information Processing & Management
papers.abstract: Generative search shifts information evaluation from comparing ranked documents to assessing synthesised answers. This study examines how users’ perceptions of answer quality are associated with trust and credibility in Google AI Overviews and explores whether visible interface cues may foster trust without systematic source verification. Study 1 analysed survey data from 510 Spanish users using a consistent partial least squares structural equation modelling approach. Study 2 combined eye tracking and interviews with 20 Spanish users. The model explained 75.7% of the variance in trust and 91.0% of the variance in credibility. Clarity and context ( β = .419, p < .001) and access to additional information and supporting sources ( β = .335, p = .002) showed the strongest observed associations with trust, whereas response immediacy was not significant ( β = .008, p = .874). Trust ( β = .834) and perceived usefulness ( β = .229) were positively associated with credibility (both p < .001), which, in turn, was associated with recommendation following ( β = .877) and intention to use ( β = .553; both p < .001). Eye tracking recorded no analysable fixations on the AI-error warning, while the interviews indicated that participants in this subsample did not routinely verify the displayed sources and often interpreted visible references as indicators of reliability. Taken together, Study 1 identifies associations between perceived answer-quality cues, trust, and credibility, whereas Study 2 suggests that visual prominence and visible references appeared to operate as authority cues for some participants and may encourage reliance without active source verification.

papers.title: A Comparative Evaluation of ChatGPT and Google Search Output for Caregiver Education in Tetralogy of Fallot
papers.venue: Cardiology and Therapy
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Caregivers of children with tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) frequently seek medical information online to better understand their child's diagnosis, treatment, and long-term care. Recently, generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, including Google AI Overview and ChatGPT, have emerged as widely accessible sources of health information. However, the quality, readability, and accuracy of these platforms for caregiver education in congenital heart disease remain poorly characterized. METHODS: Forty frequently asked caregiver questions regarding TOF were identified using Google's "People Also Ask" feature. Each question was submitted to ChatGPT-5.5 and entered as a Google search query, generating 80 total responses. Google search output comprised 37 AI Overviews and three organic search excerpts. Responses were evaluated for word count, Flesch Reading Ease (FRE), and Flesch-Kincaid grade level (FKGL). Two independent reviewers assessed response accuracy using a 5-point Likert scale, while one reviewer evaluated educational quality using a modified Ensuring Quality Information for Patients (EQIP) instrument. RESULTS: Compared with Google search output (37 AI Overviews and three organic search excerpts), ChatGPT-5.5 generated significantly longer responses (327.9 ± 117.0 vs. 192.5 ± 85.9 words, p < 0.001), with a higher reading level (FKGL: 23.7 ± 8.5 vs. 15.4 ± 3.6, p < 0.001) and lower readability (FRE: 17.3 ± 14.9 vs. 27.4 ± 11.7, p < 0.001). ChatGPT-5.5 demonstrated higher reviewer-rated accuracy (4.95 ± 0.19 vs. 4.40 ± 0.44, p < 0.001) and higher modified EQIP scores (86.44% ± 7.01% vs. 59.62% ± 13.99%, p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Under the study's prompting conditions, ChatGPT-5.5 responses received higher reviewer-rated accuracy and modified EQIP scores than Google search output but were longer and had higher calculated reading-grade levels. These findings do not establish improved caregiver comprehension, which was not directly assessed.

papers.title: Comunicação pública sob mediação algorítmica: SEO, AI Overviews e o impacto nas métricas de audiência das notícias do portal do STJ (2020-2025)
papers.venue: Revista Processus Multidisciplinar
papers.abstract: Este artigo analisa os impactos da mediação algorítmica e da incorporação de sistemas de inteligência artificial (IA) nos mecanismos de busca sobre a comunicação pública do Poder Judiciário, a partir do caso da seção de notícias do portal de notícias do Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ), no período de 2020 a 2025. Adota-se abordagem qualitativa, com estudo de caso baseado em dados institucionais de acesso e produção de conteúdo. Os resultados evidenciam dois movimentos distintos: um ciclo de expansão sustentada ao longo de quatro anos, associado à adoção de estratégias de otimização para mecanismos de busca (SEO), e uma inflexão em 2025, caracterizada pela redução no volume de acessos, sem relação com variações no volume de publicações. A análise sugere que o crescimento decorreu de ganhos de performance relacionados à visibilidade e à encontrabilidade da informação. Sob a ótica da literatura, a queda de acessos é interpretada como resultado de transformações no ecossistema informacional, especialmente com o avanço de recursos como o AI Overviews do Google e de fenômenos como o zero-click search, que reduzem a necessidade de acesso direto às fontes originárias de informação. Como contribuição, o artigo questiona a adequação dos indicadores tradicionais de desempenho e alerta para a necessidade de desenvolvimento de métricas voltadas à mensuração da visibilidade informacional em ambientes com mediação algorítmica.

papers.title: The Answer Index: what AI answer engines cite across eight industries

papers.title: SEO as a tool for managing the company's digital presence
papers.venue: Journal of Monetary Economics and Management
papers.abstract: This article explores the role of search engine optimization (SEO) as a strategic management tool for a company's digital presence. Using a comparative analysis of industry data, it examines the dynamics of the global SEO software market and the bipolar structure of the Russian search market: Yandex relies on behavioral factors, while Google prioritizes content quality and reputation. This divergence requires Russian companies to pursue two coordinated, yet distinct, optimization strategies. The ROI of digital channels is analyzed: SEO delivers the highest long-term returns, although the payback period ranges from nine to sixteen months. The impact of AI Overviews blocks is also examined: their proliferation has led to a significant drop in organic click-through rates and has brought GEO (Generative Response Evaluation) to the forefront: a strategy aimed at reaching cited sources of generative responses. papers.title: Between resistance and negotiation. Intellectual property as a survival strategy for media facing AI and digital platforms
papers.venue: OpenAlex indexed work
papers.abstract: Introduction. Generative AI has intensified tensions between news organisations and technology platforms over intellectual property, audience traffic and journalism’s economic sustainability. The report examines how leading Spanish digital media have framed AI since ChatGPT’s emergence, while considering the subsequent disruption caused by Google AI Overviews and AI Mode.Methods. The study combines quantitative content analysis with legal and industry analysis. It examines 242 AI-related articles published between January 2022 and December 2024 by leading Spanish digital-native and legacy outlets, selected according to GfK DAM audience data. Frequency distributions and contingency tables assess thematic frames and editorial positions.Results. Intellectual property emerges as the central underlying conflict. Coverage concentrates on authorship (68%), ethics and legal liability (45%), business models and licensing (32%), and employment (21%). Legacy media generally frame AI as a threat to journalistic assets, whereas digital-native outlets emphasise efficiency and commercial opportunities. Civil society and journalists themselves remain marginal in the debate. Google’s AI-generated summaries further intensify concerns by retaining users within the platform and reducing referral traffic.Discussion. Intellectual property is becoming both a defensive right and a bargaining asset. The sector is consequently shifting from litigation towards licensing, collective negotiation and technological adaptation, although confidential agreements may strengthen major publishers while marginalising smaller outlets.

papers.title: Breaking News Out of the Filter Bubble: Generative AI Search Diversifies Collective Attention and Raises Shared Information Consumption
papers.venue: arXiv
papers.abstract: Generative AI search and AI overviews are transforming access to information and news, renewing concerns that readers will encounter a narrower range of topics and have less in common. We examine these concerns via a randomized field experiment with 37,561 readers at The Washington Post. Both groups searched the same archive, but treatment readers also received AI answers with article citations above conventional results. Measuring consumption across displayed answers and opened articles, we find that AI search expands the reach of widely read topics and increases overlap in readers' topic consumption. At the same time, consumption becomes less concentrated and shifts toward less-popular topics, both within readers and across the audience. AI answers account for most of the increase in shared information, delivering it without requiring article clicks and broadening exposure beyond the articles readers open. Cited articles also contribute to the shift toward less-popular topics. Readers shift from conventional-result clicks and browsing toward cited articles and follow-up searches. More frequent searching offsets lower article consumption per search, producing a small increase in article consumption per reader. Total information consumption per minute also rises. Generative AI search can thus diversify collective attention while strengthening the information readers have in common.

papers.title: The AI Citation Gap: How Brand Demand, Authority, and Knowledge Panels Decide Which of 1,000 US Personal Injury Law Firms AI Assistants Cite
papers.venue: Figshare
papers.abstract: When a US consumer asks an AI assistant a legal question, the assistant answers with a synthesized paragraph and a short list of named entities and cited pages. Which law firms appear in those answers, and whose web pages host the citations, is rapidly becoming the discoverability question of the decade for the personal injury (PI) vertical, where a single signed case can be worth six or seven figures and a single head-term click transacts for hundreds of dollars. This paper is the eighth in a series on entity-completeness signals in the top-ranking US PI vertical. It presents, to our knowledge, the first large-N per-assistant AI citation audit of the vertical: for the same 1,000 top-ranking US personal injury law firm sample used throughout the series, we join per-firm mention and cited-page counts across four AI answer surfaces (ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overview, and Google AI Mode) to the brand-search-demand, Person Entity Panel, Google Business Panel, domain-authority, and schema-completeness signals established in the prior papers. Three findings define what we name the AI Citation Gap. First, AI visibility is extremely concentrated: the median firm receives just 22 AI mentions across all four surfaces combined, the top 100 firms absorb 51.6% of all mentions, the bottom 500 firms share 9.6%, and the Gini coefficient of the mention distribution is 0.65. Second, the four assistants agree on who matters (pairwise Spearman ρ = 0.70 to 0.88) but not symmetrically: 126 firms that are visible on Google's AI surfaces are completely absent from ChatGPT, while only 14 firms show the reverse pattern. Third, the citations are mostly not on the firm's own website. We introduce the Citation Intermediation Ratio (CIR), the share of a firm's AI citation footprint hosted by domains other than its own, and report a median CIR of 0.72: for the median firm, roughly 72% of its AI citations are hosted by third parties, with legal directories alone hosting 23%, and 99% of firms fall below 50% own-site share. Domain authority is the dominant correlate of AI mentions (ρ = 0.80), brand search demand is the strongest firm-controllable second lever (firm brand ρ = 0.44, significant in regression net of authority), the Person Entity Panel is citation-neutral, and the Google Business Panel is again associated with a citation deficit (median 19 vs 36 mentions, p < 0.001; OLS coefficient negative and significant), extending the zero-click cannibalization pattern documented in the Brand Demand Flywheel paper into the AI answer layer. An OLS model on log mentions reaches R² = 0.64. The paper closes with Citation Surface Optimization (CSO), a practitioner framework for managing owned versus rented AI citation surfaces.

papers.title: Who Does AI Cite? Reconciling Conflicting Evidence on the Sources Behind Generative Search Answers (2024–2026)
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Published studies disagree sharply about which websites generative AI search engines cite. One widely shared figure places Reddit at about 40% of citations, another reports that the most-cited domain rarely exceeds 5%, and a third claims that YouTube has overtaken Reddit. This paper asks why. It reports a structured secondary review of 30 studies and statements published between 2025 and September 2026, covering ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, AI Mode, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot and Claude. Each headline figure was traced to its original publisher and coded for metric definition, selection stage, engine, prompt universe, time window, collection method, counting unit and sponsor. Most of the disagreement comes from measurement choices. The same Profound dataset gives Wikipedia 7.8% of all ChatGPT citations and 47.9% of the top ten. Semrush's widely quoted Reddit values sum to 208%, so they cannot be shares of citations. YouTube's rise was measured within social citations, which formed only about 4% to 7% of all citations. Estimates of overlap with Google's rankings range from 12% to 91% depending on whether URLs or domains are compared. After these corrections, three findings hold. Engines differ in source mix, query type changes the mix, and citation shares move in steps after access and retrieval changes. Two conflicts remain unresolved. The paper offers a reconciliation checklist, a brand investment framework, six testable propositions and a design for a pre-registered panel study.
